reading: LTR-16: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
setup: Covered interest parity on USD/JPY, quoted in JPY per USD. Spot is 110.00. One-year rates, annually compounded: USD 2.50%, JPY 0.450%. Parity holds exactly, and the swap rate is the one-year forward minus spot, $F - S$.
ask: The swap rate $F - S$ is:

options.label: Positive: forward above spot
options.why: Put the rates on the wrong sides, using $(1+r_{USD})/(1+r_{JPY})$. The higher-yielding currency (USD) trades at a forward discount, so JPY per USD falls.

options.label: Zero
options.why: Read 'parity holds' as 'no forward points'. Parity means the forward exactly offsets the rate gap, so the forward differs from spot.

takeaway: The currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount. USD yields more than JPY, so the JPY-per-USD forward sits below spot.

reading: LTR-16: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
setup: Covered interest parity with the rate quoted in USD per EUR. Spot is 1.3988. One-year yields: EUR 2.28%, USD 3.33%. The forward equals spot times a ratio of the two gross rates $1+r$.
ask: The factor that multiplies spot to give the forward is closest to:

options.why: Inverted the ratio, using $(1+r_{EUR})/(1+r_{USD})$. With the quote in USD per EUR the USD gross rate goes on top.
Added the two yields to 1 instead of dividing the gross rates: $1 + 0.0228 + 0.0333$.

takeaway: In USD per EUR the forward is spot times $(1+r_{USD})/(1+r_{EUR})$. The higher USD yield puts the EUR at a forward premium, so the factor is above 1.

setup: Normal liquid asset buffer for a stress test, USD m. Holdings: unencumbered Treasuries 420 (stress haircut 0%), unencumbered agency MBS 200 (15%), Treasuries pledged against a wholesale borrowing 150, cash held for daily payment clearing 60, unrestricted central bank deposits 80. Gross total 910. Only free, non-operational holdings count toward the buffer.
ask: Before any haircut, the amount of the 910 that drops out is:

options.label: USD 150m
options.why: Removed the pledged Treasuries but kept the payment-clearing cash. That cash is operational liquidity, not buffer.

options.label: USD 60m
options.why: Removed only the clearing cash and kept the pledged Treasuries, which are already committed to the secured borrowing.

options.label: USD 30m
options.why: Mixed up the 15% MBS haircut with an exclusion. A haircut trims a qualifying asset; it does not remove a line.

takeaway: Pledged and operational holdings never count toward the buffer. Haircuts are applied only to what is left.

setup: 30-day stress, EUR m, with the Basel III LCR cap. Stressed outflows: retail deposits 220, unsecured wholesale 180, derivative collateral calls 60, committed-facility drawdowns 40. Stressed inflows: loan repayments 260, maturing reverse repos 160. Inflows may be counted only up to 75% of outflows. Normal buffer 520.
ask: The inflow figure that counts in the stressed buffer is:

options.label: EUR 420m
options.why: Counted every expected inflow and ignored the cap.

options.label: EUR 315m
options.why: Applied the 75% to the inflows (0.75 × 420) instead of to the outflows.

options.label: EUR 260m
options.why: Counted only the loan repayments and dropped the reverse repos. The cap limits the total, not which items qualify.

takeaway: The cap is a share of outflows. It binds only when raw inflows exceed it, here 420 against 375.

setup: Funding plan for next month, USD m. Uses of funds: new qualifying loans 220, agency MBS purchase 40, credit-line drawdowns 60. Sources: deposits received today 90, further deposit inflows expected 110. Policy adds a 10% safety margin to the estimated funding gap.
ask: The amount to plan to raise from nondeposit sources is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 12m
options.why: Reported only the safety margin, 10% of the gap, instead of the gap plus the margin.

options.label: ≈ USD 352m
options.why: Forgot to net the deposits off. Applied the 10% margin to total uses of 320.

options.label: ≈ USD 1,200m
options.why: Read the 10% margin as a factor of 10 on the gap, not 1.10 times it.

takeaway: Gap = uses minus sources, and the safety margin scales the gap, not the gross uses.

reading: LTR-16: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
setup: A BBB-rated firm needs five-year USD funding. Its bonds trade at swap + 100 bp in USD or swap + 50 bp in EUR. If it issues in EUR it swaps into USD through a cross-currency basis swap, paying a 30 bp basis on top of the USD rate. The five-year EUR swap rate is 70 bp below the USD swap rate.
ask: Relative to issuing in USD, issuing in EUR and swapping:

options.label: Saves, but by less than the 50 bp spread advantage
Saves the full 50 bp
options.why: Ignored the 30 bp basis, as if covered interest parity held with no basis.

options.label: Costs more, because of the 70 bp lower EUR swap rate
options.why: Charged the 70 bp rate-level gap against the saving. The swap converts the EUR rate level into the USD one, so that gap drops out.

working.label: EUR swapped cost
working.display: $50 + 30 = 80$ bp over the USD swap rate

takeaway: The basis eats part of the spread advantage, 30 of 50 bp here. The EUR swap rate's 70 bp discount is a red herring once the proceeds are swapped.

setup: Required stable funding (RSF) for a bank with USD 300m of assets, as amount × RSF factor: cash 20 × 0%, Treasuries (over 1 year) 20 × 5%, mortgages 50 × 65%, small-business loans 180 × 85%, fixed assets 30 × 100%.
ask: Which line contributes most to RSF?

options.label: Fixed assets
options.why: Ranked by factor alone. Fixed assets carry the top 100% factor but only 30 of balance, so 30 against 153.

options.label: Mortgages
options.why: Treated the mortgage book as the big long-term asset, but $50 \times 65\% = 32.5$ is far below the loan book.

takeaway: RSF is balance times factor. A large book at 85% beats a small book at 100%.

setup: Goodwill Bank. Funding (amount × ASF factor): retail deposits 35 × 90%, wholesale deposits 50 × 50%, Tier 2 capital 5 × 100%, Tier 1 capital 10 × 100%, other liabilities 17.5 × 0%. Assets (amount × RSF factor): cash 7 × 0%, mortgages 38 × 65%, Treasuries 6.5 × 5%, small-business loans 54 × 85%, fixed assets 12 × 100%.
ask: Against the 100% minimum, the net stable funding ratio is:

options.label: Exactly 100%
options.why: Compared unweighted totals: funding and assets both add to 117.5. The factors, not the balance sheet totals, drive NSFR.

options.label: Above 100%
options.why: Weighted only the assets (RSF 82.9) and compared them with unweighted funding of 117.5, which gives about 142%.

takeaway: NSFR weights both sides. Equal balance sheet totals say nothing: the funding carries low ASF factors while the assets are mostly high-RSF loans.

setup: ABC Bank, 2019, USD m: high-quality liquid assets 1,458; average monthly withdrawals in normal conditions 2,458; net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period 1,700.
ask: The denominator of the 2019 liquidity coverage ratio is:

options.why: Used normal-conditions withdrawals. LCR is defined against 30 days of stress, so they do not enter.
Added the normal withdrawals to the stressed outflows, double counting.

takeaway: LCR = HQLA over stressed 30-day net outflows. Normal-conditions flows are a distractor, and below 100% fails the requirement.

setup: LCR inputs, USD m. 30-day gross outflows: stable retail deposits 500 at 5% run-off, unsecured wholesale funding 300 at 40%. Expected inflows 60. Inflows may count only up to 75% of gross outflows.
ask: The inflows that count against the outflows are:

options.label: USD 108.75m
options.why: Credited the cap itself. The cap is a ceiling on counted inflows, not an allowance that tops them up.

options.label: USD 45m
options.why: Took 75% of the inflows (0.75 × 60) instead of comparing the inflows with 75% of outflows.

takeaway: The 75% cap is measured on gross outflows and only bites when inflows exceed it. Here 60 is well inside 108.75.

setup: A collateralised loan: USD 200 is lent against securities worth USD 225. The haircut is the part of collateral value not lent, as a percentage of collateral value. The USD 25 cushion is 12.5% of the USD 200 loan.
ask: The haircut, compared with 12.5%, is:

options.label: Equal to 12.5%
options.why: Divided the USD 25 cushion by the loan (25/200) instead of by the collateral value (25/225).

options.label: Higher than 12.5%
options.why: Reported the fraction lent, 200/225 = 88.9%, which is $1 - h$, not the haircut.

takeaway: Haircut = cushion over collateral value. The bigger denominator makes it smaller than the cushion over the loan.

setup: A firm earns 10% on assets of USD 7, funded by USD 2 of equity and USD 5 of debt costing 5%.
ask: Compared with the 10% return on assets, the return on equity is:

options.label: Lower than 10%
options.why: Assumed borrowing always drags returns down. Debt that costs less than ROA raises ROE.

options.label: Equal to 10%
options.why: Ignored the leverage entirely and left ROE at the asset return.

takeaway: When ROA exceeds the cost of debt, every extra unit of leverage adds the spread to ROE.

setup: A convertible-arbitrage strategy earns 11% on USD 16m of assets. It is financed 60% with borrowing at 7% and 40% with equity.
ask: The return on equity is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip (0.1×): moved the decimal when converting 17% to a decimal and back.
Multiplied the 4% spread by the debt-to-equity ratio of 1.5 and forgot to add back the 11% asset return.
Added the cost of debt to ROA on the levered amount, $2.5 \times (11+7)$, instead of subtracting it on the borrowed part.

takeaway: ROE = ROA + (D/E) × (ROA − cost of debt). Here 11% + 1.5 × 4% = 17%.

setup: Callahan has total assets of USD 5m, equity of USD 2m, ROA 7% and cost of debt 3%. It doubles its leverage ratio (assets / equity) while assets and ROA stay fixed. Each extra unit of leverage adds ROA minus the cost of debt.
ask: The rise in ROE is closest to:

options.label: 4 percentage points
options.why: Stopped at the 4% spread (7% − 3%) and did not multiply by the 2.5 extra turns of leverage.

options.label: 13 percentage points
options.why: Gave the starting ROE (2.5 × 7% − 1.5 × 3% = 13%), not the change.

options.label: 23 percentage points
options.why: Gave the new ROE level, not the increase over the old one.

takeaway: ΔROE = ΔL × (ROA − cost of debt). The 4% spread is earned on each added turn.

setup: A fund holds USD 100 cash, USD 20 bank debt and USD 80 equity, so leverage (assets / equity) is $100/80 = 1.25$. It buys USD 100 of stock at a 50% Reg T margin: USD 50 of its own cash plus a USD 50 broker loan. The broker keeps the stock as collateral.
ask: After the purchase, leverage is:

options.label: Unchanged at 1.25
options.why: Thought paying half from own cash adds no leverage. The USD 50 broker loan still enlarges assets to 150 while equity stays at 80.

options.label: Above 2.0
options.why: Added the USD 100 stock to the full USD 100 cash, forgetting that USD 50 of cash was spent. That gives assets of 200 and leverage 2.5.

takeaway: Borrowing to buy raises assets while equity is unchanged, so leverage rises. Count the cash actually spent.

setup: A fund has USD 100 cash, USD 20 debt and USD 80 equity. It shorts a stock by borrowing USD 100 of shares and selling them. The USD 100 proceeds stay in a segregated account at the broker, and the fund also posts USD 50 of margin from its cash.
ask: Total assets after the trade are closest to:

options.label: USD 100
options.why: Counted only the remaining cash and the margin (50 + 50) and left out the USD 100 of proceeds. They are an asset, matched by a USD 100 borrowed-stock liability.

options.label: USD 150
options.why: Treated the margin as leaving the balance sheet. It becomes a USD 50 receivable from the broker.

options.label: USD 250
options.why: Kept the full USD 100 cash as well as the broker balances, forgetting that the margin came out of that cash.

takeaway: A short sale grosses up the balance sheet: proceeds and margin are both receivables from the broker.

setup: A manager holds 30,000 shares of a stock that trades 70,000 shares a day. Policy caps trading at 18% of daily volume. Liquidity duration is days to exit: position size divided by the shares that may be sold per day.
ask: Liquidity duration is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 0.024 days
options.why: Entered the 18% cap as 18 instead of 0.18, giving $30{,}000/(18 \times 70{,}000)$.

options.label: ≈ 0.43 days
options.why: Divided by the whole daily volume and ignored the 18% cap.

options.label: ≈ 238 days
options.why: Read the 18% cap as 0.18%, so the daily capacity is only 126 shares.

takeaway: Exit time = position over the tradeable slice of volume. Applying the cap makes it longer than position over total volume.

setup: Term structure of expected liquidity under stress, USD m. Normal annual inflows are 795 and outflows 230. In the stress scenario inflows fall 25% and outflows rise 40%.
ask: Stressed net cash flow (inflows − outflows) for the year is closest to:

options.label: USD 366m
options.why: Cut the inflows by 25% but left the outflows at 230.

options.label: USD 565m
options.why: Used the normal-conditions figures, 795 − 230, with no stress applied.

options.label: USD 856m
options.why: Applied the shocks in the wrong direction: inflows +25% and outflows −40%.

takeaway: Stress shrinks inflows and grows outflows, so net flow falls by more than half here, from 565 to 274.

reading: LTR-10: Liquidity Risk Reporting and Stress Testing
setup: FSA liquidity-ratio treatment of off-balance-sheet items, USD m. The bank has committed but undrawn lending facilities of 600, derivatives with a notional of 2,000, and a coupon of 5 payable on a derivative inside the reporting period.
ask: The cash outflow to include for these items is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 5m
options.why: Counted only the derivative coupon and left out the 10% at-sight outflow on undrawn commitments.

options.label: ≈ USD 605m
options.why: Counted the whole undrawn facility (600) plus the coupon. Only 10% of undrawn commitments counts.

options.label: ≈ USD 2,065m
options.why: Brought in the derivative notional. Only coupons on their pay dates count, not notionals.

takeaway: Undrawn lines count at 10%. Derivatives bring in only their coupons, never the notional.

setup: A newly issued on-the-run bond with market value USD 1,000 trades special at a 0.50% a year spread from 1 July to 31 October 2019 (122 days), and at general collateral afterwards. Day count is actual/360.
ask: The financing value per USD 1,000 is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.42
options.why: Counted only the 30 days left in July instead of the full 122-day special period.

options.label: ≈ USD 5.0
options.why: Took a full year of the 0.50% spread, $1{,}000 \times 0.005$, with no day-count proration.

options.label: ≈ USD 17
options.why: Read the 0.50% spread as 5.0%, giving ten times the right value.

takeaway: Financing value is the special spread earned only for the days it applies: spread × days/360 × market value.
